title: Die faule Spinnerin
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 128. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 128 is a small domestic comedy: a wife too lazy to ever finish her spinning tricks her husband twice over, first frightening him out of the forest with a sung warning that whoever cuts reel-wood, or whoever reels, will die, and later swapping her yarn for a lump of tow while it boils so that he gives up asking about her spinning for good. Nobody is punished and the trick works completely; the narrator's dry closing remark — that she was simply a disagreeable wife — is the whole moral offered. It is one of the shortest and lightest tales in the collection.

sentences.t: Auf einem Dorfe lebte ein Mann und eine Frau, und die Frau war so faul, daß sie immer nichts arbeiten wollte:
sentences.l: In a village lived a man and a woman, and the woman was so lazy that she always wanted to work at nothing:
sentences.i: In a village there lived a man and his wife, and the wife was so lazy that she never wanted to do a stroke of work:
sentences.n: “Auf einem Dorfe” — German puts you on a village rather than in one when the village is where you live. “immer nichts arbeiten wollte” piles the negative onto the always: she wanted to work at nothing, ever. Frau does duty for both woman and wife. The colon opens the account of what her laziness came to.

sentences.t: und was ihr der Mann zu spinnen gab, das spann sie nicht fertig, und was sie auch spann, haspelte sie nicht, sondern ließ alles auf dem Klauel gewickelt liegen.
sentences.l: and what the man gave her to spin, that she did not spin finished, and what she did spin, she did not wind off, but let it all lie wound on the ball.
sentences.i: and whatever her husband gave her to spin she never finished spinning, and what she did spin she never wound off, but let it all lie there wound on the ball.
sentences.n: The spinning matters, and the tale does not work if the picture is wrong. Thread comes off the wheel onto a Klauel, a ball; it then has to be wound off — haspeln — onto a Haspel, a reel, before it can be boiled and used. She stops at the ball. “was … das” is the ordinary German frame: what he gave her, that she left unfinished.

sentences.t: Schalt sie nun der Mann, so war sie mit ihrem Maul doch vornen, und sprach „ei, wie sollt ich haspeln, da ich keinen Haspel habe, geh du erst in den Wald und schaff mir einen.“
sentences.l: If the man now scolded her, she was with her mouth out in front all the same, and spoke “ah, how should I wind off, when I have no reel? you go first into the wood and get me one.”
sentences.i: If her husband scolded her, she was quick enough with her mouth all the same, and said: “Now how am I to wind off, when I have no reel? You go into the wood first and get me one.”
sentences.n: “Schalt sie nun der Mann” puts the verb first with no wenn — German can open a condition that way, and English has to put the if back in. “mit dem Maul vornen sein” is to be out in front with your mouth, ready with an answer; das Maul is an animal’s mouth, and of a person it is coarse. She turns the scolding into an errand for him.

sentences.t: „Wenns daran liegt,“ sagte der Mann, „so will ich in den Wald gehen und Haspelholz holen.“
sentences.l: “If it lies on that,” said the man, “then I will go into the wood and fetch reel-wood.”
sentences.i: “If that is all it is,” said the man, “then I will go into the wood and fetch wood for a reel.”
sentences.n: “daran liegen” = to depend on that, to be the thing at issue; “wenns” is wenn es. Haspelholz is coined on the spot — wood for a reel — and it carries the rest of the tale.

sentences.t: Da fürchtete sich die Frau, wenn er das Holz hätte, daß er daraus einen Haspel machte, und sie abhaspeln und dann wieder frisch spinnen müßte.
sentences.l: Then the woman feared, if he had the wood, that he would make a reel out of it, and she would have to wind off and then spin fresh again.
sentences.i: Then the wife grew afraid that if he had the wood he would make a reel of it, and she would have to wind off her yarn and then start spinning afresh.
sentences.n: sich fürchten is reflexive — she fears herself, as it were. The subjunctives hätte and machte are the shape of her imagining: if he had it, he would make one. abhaspeln is to wind the whole lot off (ab- = off), which is exactly the work she is dodging.

sentences.t: Sie besann sich ein bischen, da kam ihr ein guter Einfall, und sie lief dem Manne heimlich nach in den Wald.
sentences.l: She bethought herself a little, then a good idea came to her, and she ran after the man secretly into the wood.
sentences.i: She thought for a moment, and a good idea came to her, and she ran secretly after her husband into the wood.
sentences.n: ein Einfall is what falls in on you — a notion arriving of itself, from einfallen. bischen is the 1857 spelling of bisschen. nachlaufen is separable and takes the dative: she ran after the man, dem Manne.

sentences.t: Wie er nun auf einen Baum gestiegen war, das Holz auszulesen und zu hauen, schlich sie darunter in das Gebüsch, wo er sie nicht sehen konnte und rief hinauf
sentences.l: When he had now climbed up a tree, to pick out the wood and to hew it, she crept beneath into the bushes, where he could not see her, and called up
sentences.i: When he had climbed a tree to pick out the wood and cut it, she crept in below into the bushes, where he could not see her, and called up:
sentences.n: wie here is when, not how. auslesen is to pick out (aus- + lesen, to gather); hauen is to hew. The sentence has no full stop — it runs straight on into the verse.

sentences.t:
„wer Haspelholz haut, der stirbt,
wer da haspelt der verdirbt.“
sentences.l:
“whoever hews reel-wood, he dies,
whoever winds off there, he perishes.”
sentences.i:
“Whoever cuts wood for a reel dies;
whoever winds off comes to ruin.”
sentences.n: Two lines that do the whole work of the tale. haut is from hauen, to hew — not from die Haut, skin, which is spelt the same. “wer … der” is the old relative pattern: whoever does this, that one dies. The German rhymes stirbt / verdirbt; verderben is to spoil, to come to ruin. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme — the rhyme stays in the German.

sentences.t: Der Mann horchte, legte die Axt eine Weile nieder und dachte nach was das wohl zu bedeuten hätte.
sentences.l: The man listened, laid the axe down for a while and thought after what that might well have to mean.
sentences.i: The man listened, laid the axe down a while and pondered what that could be supposed to mean.
sentences.n: niederlegen and nachdenken are both separable, and both particles have swung to the end of their clauses: legte … nieder, dachte nach. The subjunctive hätte makes it his wondering rather than a fact.

sentences.t: „Ei was,“ sprach er endlich, „was wirds gewesen sein! es hat dir in den Ohren geklungen, mache dir keine unnöthige Furcht.“
sentences.l: “Ah what,” he spoke at last, “what will it have been! it has rung in your ears, make yourself no unnecessary fear.”
sentences.i: “Oh, nonsense,” he said at last, “what could it have been! Your ears were ringing — do not go frightening yourself for nothing.”
sentences.n: “Ei was” is a brush-off: oh, come now. “was wirds gewesen sein” uses the future of werden to shrug at the past — what will it have been, i.e. it cannot have been anything. He talks to himself as du, which is where the dir comes from. unnöthige is the 1857 spelling of unnötige.

sentences.t: Also ergriff er die Axt von neuem und wollte zuhauen, da riefs wieder von unten herauf
sentences.l: So he seized the axe anew and wanted to strike, then it called again from below up
sentences.i: So he took up the axe again and made to strike, and again it called up from below:
sentences.n: zuhauen is to lay on with the axe (zu- as in zugreifen, to set to work). riefs is rief es, the clitic es glued onto the verb — a voice with nobody named to own it, which is what makes it eerie.

sentences.t:
„wer Haspelholz haut, der stirbt,
wer da haspelt der verdirbt.“
sentences.l:
“whoever hews reel-wood, he dies,
whoever winds off there, he perishes.”
sentences.i:
“Whoever cuts wood for a reel dies;
whoever winds off comes to ruin.”
sentences.n: The same two lines again, word for word — the second of three. Their force is in the repetition, and in his having no idea who is speaking.

sentences.t: Er hielt ein, kriegte angst und bang und sann dem Ding nach.
sentences.l: He held in, got afraid and anxious and thought after the thing.
sentences.i: He stopped, grew frightened and uneasy, and turned the thing over in his mind.
sentences.n: einhalten is to stop, to break off (hielt … ein). “angst und bang” is a fixed pair, two words for fear doubled for weight; bang is at home in the north but stands here in a High German tale. nachsinnen takes the dative — dem Ding, to brood over a thing.

sentences.t: Wie aber ein Weilchen vorbei war, kam ihm das Herz wieder, und er langte zum drittenmal nach der Axt und wollte zuhauen.
sentences.l: But when a little while was past, the heart came back to him, and he reached for the third time after the axe and wanted to strike.
sentences.i: But when a little while had passed, his heart came back to him, and he reached for the axe a third time and made to strike.
sentences.n: “kam ihm das Herz wieder” — the dative ihm where English wants a possessive: his heart came back, that is, his courage returned. Weilchen is the diminutive of Weile, a little while.

sentences.t: Aber zum drittenmale riefs und sprachs laut
sentences.l: But for the third time it called and it spoke loud
sentences.i: But a third time it called and spoke aloud:
sentences.n: riefs and sprachs are rief es and sprach es. The tale writes zum drittenmal a line above and zum drittenmale here; 1857 does not fuss over the old dative -e.

sentences.t:
„wer Haspelholz haut, der stirbt,
wer da haspelt der verdirbt.“
sentences.l:
“whoever hews reel-wood, he dies,
whoever winds off there, he perishes.”
sentences.i:
“Whoever cuts wood for a reel dies;
whoever winds off comes to ruin.”
sentences.n: The third time, and it is what breaks him — three is the number these tales count to.

sentences.t: Da hatte ers genug, und alle Lust war ihm vergangen, so daß er eilends den Baum herunter stieg und sich auf den Heimweg machte.
sentences.l: Then he had it enough, and all desire had passed away from him, so that he hastily climbed down the tree and made himself onto the homeward way.
sentences.i: By then he had had enough, and all his appetite for it was gone, so that he climbed down the tree in haste and set off for home.
sentences.n: “die Lust vergeht mir” is the standing idiom — the appetite for a thing passes away from you, with the person in the dative (ihm). “sich auf den Heimweg machen” is to set out for home.

sentences.t: Die Frau lief, was sie konnte, auf Nebenwegen, damit sie eher nach Haus käme.
sentences.l: The woman ran what she could, on side-ways, so that she might come home sooner.
sentences.i: The wife ran as hard as she could by side paths, so as to be home before him.
sentences.n: “lief, was sie konnte” = ran what she was able to. Nebenwege are the paths off to the side (neben-), taken so as to overtake him unseen; the subjunctive käme belongs to the damit clause of purpose.

sentences.t: Wie er nun in die Stube trat, that sie unschuldig, als wäre nichts vorgefallen, und sagte „nun, bringst du ein gutes Haspelholz?“
sentences.l: When he now stepped into the room, she did innocent, as if nothing had happened, and said “well, do you bring a good reel-wood?”
sentences.i: When he came into the room, she put on an innocent face, as if nothing had happened, and said: “Well, have you brought a good piece of reel-wood?”
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat — thun, thut, that for tun, tut, tat run through all these tales. “unschuldig thun” is to act innocent; “als wäre nichts vorgefallen” is the subjunctive after als with no wenn: as if nothing had occurred.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sprach er, „ich sehe wohl, es geht mit dem Haspeln nicht,“ erzählte ihr was ihm im Walde begegnet war und ließ sie von nun an damit in Ruhe.
sentences.l: “No,” he spoke, “I see well, it goes not with the winding,” told her what had met him in the wood and let her from now on be in peace with it.
sentences.i: “No,” said he, “I can see the winding is not going to work,” and he told her what had happened to him in the wood, and left her in peace about it from then on.
sentences.n: “es geht nicht” = it will not do. begegnen takes the dative — what met him. She has won the first round without lifting a finger.

sentences.t: Bald hernach fieng der Mann doch wieder an sich über die Unordnung im Hause zu ärgern.
sentences.l: Soon thereafter the man began all the same again to vex himself over the disorder in the house.
sentences.i: Soon after, though, the man began once more to be annoyed at the disorder in the house.
sentences.n: anfangen is separable, and its two parts sit at opposite ends: fieng … an, with the whole sentence between. fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: „Frau,“ sagte er, „es ist doch eine Schande, daß das gesponnene Garn da auf dem Klauel liegen bleibt.“
sentences.l: “Wife,” said he, “it is a shame after all, that the spun yarn there stays lying on the ball.”
sentences.i: “Wife,” said he, “it is a disgrace that the spun yarn just lies there on the ball.”
sentences.n: He calls her simply Frau, the ordinary way a husband addressed his wife. gesponnene is the past participle of spinnen used as an adjective; “liegen bleiben” is to be left lying.

sentences.t: „Weißt du was,“ sprach sie, „weil wir doch zu keinem Haspel kommen, so stell dich auf den Boden und ich steh unten, da will ich dir den Klauel hinauf werfen, und du wirfst ihn herunter, so gibts doch einen Strang.“
sentences.l: “Do you know what,” she spoke, “since we come to no reel anyway, then set yourself up in the loft and I stand below, then I will throw you the ball up, and you throw it down, so there is a skein after all.”
sentences.i: “I will tell you what,” she said, “since we are never going to get a reel, go and stand up in the loft while I stand below; then I will throw the ball up to you and you throw it down again, and that will make a skein.”
sentences.n: der Boden here is not the ground but the loft, the floor under the roof (as in Dachboden) — which is why he goes up and she stays below. “zu etwas kommen” is to get hold of a thing; der Strang is a skein. What she proposes is nonsense dressed as a plan: tossing a ball to and fro winds nothing at all.

sentences.t: „Ja, das geht,“ sagte der Mann.
sentences.l: “Yes, that goes,” said the man.
sentences.i: “Yes, that will do,” said the man.
sentences.n: “das geht” = that works, that will do — the same idiom he used in the negative a moment ago.

sentences.t: Also thaten sie das, und wie sie fertig waren, sprach er „das Garn ist nun gesträngt, nun muß es auch gekocht werden.“
sentences.l: So they did that, and when they were finished, he spoke “the yarn is now skeined, now it must also be boiled.”
sentences.i: So they did it, and when they had finished he said: “The yarn is skeined now; now it has to be boiled as well.”
sentences.n: thaten is the 1857 spelling of taten. strängen, to make into a skein, is formed straight off der Strang. Boiling came next in the real work: yarn was boiled to clean and set it — and it is the step she now has to escape.

sentences.t: Der Frau ward wieder angst, sie sprach zwar „ja wir wollens gleich morgen früh kochen,“ dachte aber bei sich auf einen neuen Streich.
sentences.l: To the woman it became afraid again, she spoke indeed “yes we will boil it right away tomorrow morning,” but thought to herself on a new trick.
sentences.i: The wife grew frightened again; she said, to be sure, “yes, we will boil it first thing tomorrow morning,” but was thinking to herself of a new trick.
sentences.n: “der Frau ward angst” is impersonal with the person in the dative: it grew fearful to her. ward is the old form of wurde. ein Streich is a trick or a prank, not a stroke of the hand, and “auf einen Streich denken” is to be plotting one. zwar … aber sets the said against the thought. morgen here is tomorrow, the adverb, not der Morgen.

sentences.t: Frühmorgens stand sie auf, machte Feuer an und stellte den Kessel bei, allein statt des Garns legte sie einen Klumpen Werg hinein, und ließ es immer zu kochen.
sentences.l: Early in the morning she stood up, made fire on and set the kettle by, only instead of the yarn she laid a lump of tow in, and let it boil on and on.
sentences.i: Early in the morning she got up, lit the fire and put the kettle on, only instead of the yarn she put in a lump of tow, and let it boil on and on.
sentences.n: Three separable verbs in a row, each with its particle at the end of the clause: stand … auf, machte … an, stellte … bei. das Werg is tow — the short tangled fibre combed out of flax and left over from spinning, worth next to nothing. That it is in the kettle instead of yarn is the whole trick. “immer zu” (modern immerzu) is on and on, without stopping. allein here means only, but — an older use.

sentences.t: Darauf gieng sie zum Manne, der noch zu Bette lag, und sprach zu ihm „ich muß einmal ausgehen, steh derweil auf und sieh nach dem Garn, das im Kessel überm Feuer steht:
sentences.l: Thereupon she went to the man, who was still lying in bed, and spoke to him “I must go out for once, get up meanwhile and look after the yarn that stands in the kettle over the fire:
sentences.i: Then she went to her husband, who was still lying in bed, and said to him: “I have to go out for a while; get up meanwhile and see to the yarn that is in the kettle over the fire.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. “nach etwas sehen” is to see to a thing, keep an eye on it; derweil = meanwhile. Every word of her instruction sounds helpful and is a trap.

sentences.t: aber du mußts bei Zeit thun, gib wohl Acht, denn wo der Hahn kräht, und du sähest nicht nach, wird das Garn zu Werg.“
sentences.l: but you must do it in good time, give good heed, for where the cock crows, and you did not look after it, the yarn turns to tow.”
sentences.i: but you must do it in good time, take good care, for if the cock crows and you have not looked, the yarn will turn to tow.”
sentences.n: mußts is mußt es; “bei Zeit” = in good time; “Acht geben” is to pay heed. wo here does duty for wenn, if — a country use — and sähest is the subjunctive of sehen inside a rule she has invented on the spot. There is no such rule: yarn does not turn to tow, and the reader already knows what is in the kettle.

sentences.t: Der Mann war bei der Hand und wollte nichts versäumen, stand eilends auf, so schnell er konnte, und gieng in die Küche.
sentences.l: The man was at hand and wanted to miss nothing, stood up hastily, as fast as he could, and went into the kitchen.
sentences.i: The man was ready and willing and meant to let nothing slip; he got up in haste, as fast as he could, and went into the kitchen.
sentences.n: “bei der Hand sein” is to be on hand, prompt. versäumen is to miss a thing by being too late — the very fear she planted in him.

sentences.t: Wie er aber zum Kessel kam und hinein sah, so erblickte er mit Schrecken nichts als einen Klumpen Werg.
sentences.l: But when he came to the kettle and looked in, he caught sight with fright of nothing but a lump of tow.
sentences.i: But when he came to the kettle and looked in, he saw to his horror nothing but a lump of tow.
sentences.n: erblicken is to catch sight of, a shade sharper than sehen; “nichts als” = nothing but. The so before erblickte is the resumptive so German likes after a leading clause, and English simply leaves it out.

sentences.t: Da schwieg der arme Mann mäuschenstill, dachte er hätts versehen und wäre Schuld daran und sprach in Zukunft gar nicht mehr von Garn und Spinnen.
sentences.l: Then the poor man kept mouse-still silent, thought he had bungled it and was to blame for it, and spoke in future not at all any more of yarn and spinning.
sentences.i: Then the poor man held his peace, quiet as a mouse, thinking he had bungled it and was to blame, and never spoke of yarn or spinning again.
sentences.n: mäuschenstill is built on the diminutive of Maus. hätts is hätte es, and the subjunctives hätte and wäre mark what he thought rather than what was so. “Schuld sein an etwas” = to be to blame for a thing. The trick has cost him not only the yarn but his own judgement.

sentences.t: Aber das mußt du selbst sagen, es war eine garstige Frau.
sentences.l: But that you must say yourself, she was a nasty woman.
sentences.i: But you must say so yourself: she was a nasty woman.
sentences.n: The teller turns and speaks to you in the last line — one of the few places in these tales where the narrator addresses the listener directly as du. garstig is nasty, ill-natured. Nothing befalls her; the tale simply says what she was and stops.

glossary.allein: allein — but, only (older use as a conjunction: “allein statt des Garns …” = only, instead of the yarn …); elsewhere alone
glossary.bang: bang — anxious, afraid (in the fixed pair “angst und bang”)
glossary.boden: der Boden — the loft, the floor under the roof (“auf den Boden” = up into the loft); elsewhere also ground, floor
glossary.es: es — it; also the impersonal it (“es geht nicht” = it will not do; “es war eine garstige Frau”)
glossary.guter: gut — good (adj., masc. nom.: “ein guter Einfall” = a good idea)
glossary.haut: hauen — hews, chops (3rd sg. present; not die Haut, skin, which is spelt the same)
glossary.immer: immer — always; in “immer zu” (modern immerzu) on and on, without stopping
glossary.morgen: morgen — tomorrow (adverb: “gleich morgen früh” = first thing tomorrow morning); also der Morgen, the morning
glossary.riefs: rufen — it called (rief es, the clitic es glued onto the verb: “da riefs wieder von unten herauf”)
glossary.streich: der Streich — a trick, a prank (“auf einen Streich denken” = to be plotting one)
glossary.wo: wo — where; in country speech also when, if (“wo der Hahn kräht” = if the cock crows)
